# Identifying the Secondary Throttle Valve on an AISAN Carburetor

You have successfully disassembled your 1987 Toyota Tercel's Aisan 14120 two-barrel carburetor and identified almost every component, yet one specific assembly remains a mystery. Based on your descriptionâspecifically that the chamber connects to the secondary barrel throat via a single orifice and terminates at the intake manifold with an internal plate-like valveâyou have encountered the **secondary throttle control valve**, often referred to as the secondary venturi valve or simply the power valve actuator assembly.

This component is distinct from the secondary throttle diaphragm you mentioned. While the diaphragm provides the mechanical linkage to open the secondary butterflies, this specific chamber and valve handle the critical function of metering fuel delivery during high-load conditions. The single orifice you noted is the feed for the secondary circuit, ensuring that fuel only enters when the engine demands it beyond the primary cylinder's capacity.

## How the Valve Operates

The mechanism inside this chamber functions as a sophisticated bypass system designed to optimize air-fuel ratios under load. When the throttle plates in the secondary barrels are wide open (typically above 60-70% opening), the vacuum signal changes drastically. This pressure differential acts upon the internal plate-like valve you observed.

In its resting state, this valve restricts or blocks the flow of fuel and air into the secondary venturi. However, as engine load increases and the throttle opens wider, the vacuum drops while manifold pressure rises. This shift triggers the valve to pivot or lift, opening a passage that allows additional fuel to mix with the incoming air stream. The result is a richer mixture required for acceleration and climbing grades.

The connection to the intake manifold at the other end of the assembly confirms its role in responding directly to engine load. Unlike the primary circuit, which maintains a relatively constant idle speed and low-load cruising efficiency, this secondary path is purely performance-oriented. It prevents the lean conditions that would occur if the primary jets were trying to supply fuel for a high-flow demand alone.

## Diagnostic Considerations and Repair Pitfalls

When reassembling this carburetor after repair, precision with this specific chamber is non-negotiable. The gasket sealing the top of this chamber is critical; any leakage here will allow unmetered air to bypass the venturi. This "unmetered air leak" will cause a lean condition under load, leading to hesitation, misfiring, or a complete lack of power when you accelerate hard.

The internal plate valve itself can be fragile. During reassembly, ensure that you do not drop debris into the chamber from the carburetor body above it. Even a single speck of dust can jam the valve plate in the closed position, rendering the secondary circuit useless permanently. If this happens, your car will behave as if it has a failed power valve, exhibiting poor throttle response and potential overheating due to running lean under high load.

Furthermore, verify that the orifice feeding this chamber is not clogged with varnish or debris from the fuel tank. Since this path handles the bulk of the fuel flow during acceleration, any restriction here will manifest as a delay in power delivery. Clean the orifice thoroughly and inspect the valve seat for wear. If the seating surface is pitted, the valve may leak slightly even when closed, causing an inconsistency in idle quality once the engine warms up.

While detailed schematics for obscure carburetors like the Aisan 14120 are rare compared to modern fuel injection systems, understanding the physics of this bypass valve allows you to diagnose issues without relying solely on manuals. If your Tercel exhibits stumbling under acceleration after a rebuild, suspect this secondary valve assembly before replacing expensive ignition components.
